% ---- a braille cell, drawn from its dot numbers ----------------------
% The paper's braille is drawn from the same dot numbers the embosser is
% sent, so a figure here cannot disagree with a figure on paper.
\newcommand{\bcell}[1]{%
  \begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=-0.55ex, x=1.75mm, y=1.75mm]
    % the six positions, faint, so an unraised dot is visible as a position
    \foreach \x/\y in {0/2, 0/1, 0/0, 1/2, 1/1, 1/0}
      {\fill[black!17] (\x,\y) circle (0.20);}
    % dot d sits in column (d>3) and row (d-1) mod 3, counting down from the top
    \foreach \d in {#1}{%
      \pgfmathsetmacro{\cx}{\d > 3 ? 1 : 0}%
      \pgfmathsetmacro{\cy}{2 - int(mod(\d - 1, 3))}%
      \fill (\cx,\cy) circle (0.44);}
  \end{tikzpicture}%
}

\title{\bfseries Standard Sindhi Braille in software:\\
implementing and verifying a ratified national braille code}

\author{%
  Safeer Ali Mirani\thanks{Corresponding author. Digital implementation,

  the Blind (Sindh); member of the committee that authored the code. Authority

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent
Standard Sindhi Braille was ratified on 7 November 2016 by a committee of the
Sindhi Language Authority, and has been taught in schools and read by touch in
Sindh ever since. Until the work reported here it existed only on paper: no
software could produce a line of it, and \texttt{liblouis}, the open braille
library behind most screen readers and embossers, shipped no table for Sindhi in
the Perso-Arabic script that Pakistan writes. We report the first digital
implementation of that code. The central difficulty is structural rather than
notational. Sindhi has \NLetters{} letters and the code must express \NMeanings{}
distinct marks, against the 63 cells a six-dot braille cell can form, so the
forward map is a function and its inverse is not: \NShared{} cells carry more
than one reading and \NThreeWay{} carry three or more. We give the resolution
procedure, which is positional for all but one case, lexical for that one, and
we report what it costs. The implementation comprises a reference translator, a
pair of \texttt{liblouis} tables, and an independent browser engine written to
the same specification so that the two can be made to disagree. Verification runs
at five levels, from the code checking itself against the committee's printed
book to the level that actually settles the question: on 15 August 2026 the
second author read an embossed page produced by this software, cold, by touch,
complete and without error. We also report four points on which the printed
standard contradicts itself, which are matters for the Authority rather than for
us.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

A braille code is not software. It is a decision, taken by people, about which
of the sixty-three arrangements of six raised dots stands for which mark of a
writing system. Once taken, the decision has to be implemented, or it reaches
almost nobody: a code that no program knows cannot be produced by a screen
reader, cannot be embossed from a file, and cannot turn a document into
something a blind reader can hold.

Sindhi is written by roughly thirty million people, principally in the Pakistani
province of Sindh, in a Perso-Arabic script of \NLetters{} letters. Its braille
code was settled in 2016 and is in daily use. Its implementation status, until
this work, was nil.

This paper reports that implementation and, more importantly, how it was checked.
We think the checking is the transferable part. A braille code for a
low-resource language is an unusual object to implement, because it is defined
entirely by a printed document and a small number of people who read it by
touch, and neither a test suite nor a corpus can substitute for either. What we
describe is a way of arranging the evidence so that each level catches a kind of
error the others cannot.

\subsection{Contributions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item The first digital implementation of Standard Sindhi Braille: a reference
      translator in both directions, \texttt{liblouis} tables for Grade 1 and
      Grade 2, and an independent browser engine.
\item A formal statement of the shared-cell problem for this code, with counts
      derived from the tables rather than asserted, and a resolution procedure
      whose one irreducible case we characterise exactly.
\item A five-level verification design, and its results, including the outcome
      of a reading by touch by a blind reader who is also an author of the code.
\item Four self-contradictions in the printed standard, reported rather than
      silently resolved.
\end{enumerate}

\section{The code and where it comes from}

Standard Sindhi Braille was given final form on 7 November 2016 under the
patronage of the Sindhi Language Authority, an autonomous institution of the
Government of Sindh. A committee of six agreed it unanimously: Prof.\ Dr Abdul
Ghafoor Memon (Chairman), Shahid Ahmed Memon (Convener), Riaz Hussain Memon,
Prof.\ Mehrab Ali Lakho, Dr Saira Saleem Khan and Shamsuddin Shaikh. The
Government of Sindh prints school textbooks in the code through the DEPD Braille
Press, Karachi.

The code is documented in the Authority's printed guide and in the second
author's Grade 1 and Grade 2 teaching books. Everything implemented here comes
from those documents. We have altered nothing: where the printed material is
ambiguous we say so in \S\ref{sec:contradictions} rather than choosing quietly.

\section{The gap}

A braille code becomes usable at scale only when software knows it. Three things
in particular were missing for Sindhi.

\emph{No table in the open braille library.} \texttt{liblouis} ships tables for
more than a hundred languages, including Arabic, Persian and Urdu, and had none
for Sindhi. A screen reader on a Sindhi page therefore had nothing to send to a
braille display.

\emph{No translator.} Producing a page of Sindhi braille meant a person
transcribing it, mark by mark.

\emph{No specification a programmer could work from.} The code existed as a
printed guide in Sindhi, which is the correct form for teachers and the wrong
form for an implementation.

\section{Why the problem is hard}

\subsection{More to say than there are cells}

A six-dot cell has $2^{6}-1 = 63$ non-empty forms. Counting only those marks the
code writes as a single cell on its own, our implementation assigns
\NMeanings{} distinct meanings across \NCellsUsed{} of those 63 forms. Including
marks written as two cells, every one of the 63 is used.

Let $\Sigma$ be the set of marks the code must express and $\mathcal{B}$ the set
of cells. Forward translation is a map
\[
T:\Sigma^{*}\longrightarrow\mathcal{B}^{*},
\]
which is well defined and total. It is not injective. Because $|\Sigma| >
|\mathcal{B}|$, the pigeonhole argument alone guarantees collisions, and the code
has them: \NShared{} cells carry more than one reading and \NThreeWay{} carry
three or more. The two worst are
\[
R(\text{dot }2)=\{\,\text{zabar},\ \sdm{،},\ \text{decimal point},\
\text{lower }1,\ \text{pen-name mark}\,\}
\]
\[
R(\text{dots }2\text{-}3\text{-}6)=\{\,\sdm{ھ},\ \sdm{؟},\ \text{lower }8,\
\text{open quote}\,\}.
\]

Back-translation is therefore not the application of an inverse function. Given
$\beta \in \mathcal{B}^{*}$ it is the problem of finding some $w$ with
$T(w)=\beta$, and choosing among the candidates.

\subsection{Position resolves almost everything}

The code is built so that most collisions are resolved by where a cell sits. We
state these as predicates on the index. The clearest case is dots 3-4-5-6:
\[
c = 3456 \;\longmapsto\;
\begin{cases}
\text{number sign} & \text{if } i = 0\\
\sdm{ڻ} & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
This rule is sound only if no ordinary Sindhi word begins with \sd{ڻ}. We
tested the claim rather than assuming it, and the result is more useful than a
bare confirmation would have been. Over 23{,}432 word tokens drawn from the
committee's own publications, \sd{ڻ} occurs 604 times inside or at the end of a
word, and 18 times at the start of a token. Seventeen of those 18 are the bare
letter standing alone, which is what a book about the alphabet contains rather
than what running prose does. The eighteenth is the aspirate \sd{ڻھ}.

That single exception is not a surprise waiting to be found: \sd{ڻھ} is one of
the four spellings the round-trip check already reports as not surviving
(\S\ref{sec:suite}), because its two cells are also the fraction $1/8$. The
positional rule is therefore sound for prose, and its one failure is already
counted in the fidelity figure rather than hidden behind it. We would rather
report a rule with a measured exception than a rule with none.

Dots 2-5-6, 2-3-5 and 2 resolve on word-final position; dots 2-5 resolves by
look-ahead, since a ratio is followed by a fresh number sign and a fraction
denominator is not.

\subsection{One case that position cannot resolve}
\label{sec:irreducible}

At the end of a word, dots 2-3-6 is either the letter \sd{ھ} or the question
mark \sd{؟}, and the guide places the question mark in exactly the position a
final \sd{ھ} occupies. No positional predicate separates them. Here the software
makes a decision rather than applying a rule: given the stem $s$ and a lexicon
$W$,
\[
\hat{x} =
\begin{cases}
\sdm{ھ} & \text{if } s\cdot\sdm{ھ} \in W\\
\sdm{؟} & \text{else if } s \in W\\
\sdm{ھ} & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
A human reader resolves this from the sense of the sentence. A machine, lacking
that, uses the lexicon; where the lexicon is silent it falls back on the prior,
final \sd{ھ} being far the commoner. We report this as a limitation and not as a
solved problem.

\subsection{Some rules need the whole sentence}

A cell-by-cell substitution gets Sindhi most of the way and then fails, because
several rules are not local. A repeated word is written once with a doubling
mark. A date is not a sequence of digits with separators but a construction of
its own. A fraction places the numerator in upper digits and the denominator in
lower ones, which are different cells for the same digits, so the reader must
know which half of the fraction they are in. Each of these requires the
translator to hold state across a span longer than one character, which is why
the implementation is a transducer rather than a table.

\section{Implementation}

Three implementations exist, deliberately.

\paragraph{The reference translator.} Python, both directions, Grade 1 and
Grade 2. It is the definition in the sense that the other two are checked
against it.

\paragraph{The \texttt{liblouis} tables.} A shared core
(\texttt{sd-pk-g1-core.uti}) with a Grade 1 table (\texttt{sd-pk-g1.utb}) and a
Grade 2 table (\texttt{sd-pk-g2.ctb}). Both compile without error under
\texttt{liblouis} 3.29.0, and the accompanying suite passes 99 tests with 0
failures. This is the artefact that lets a screen reader or an embosser use the
code without knowing anything about this project.

\paragraph{The browser engine.} An independent implementation in JavaScript, so
that a translator runs with nothing installed and nothing uploaded. Its purpose
in the verification design is that it can disagree with the Python. It is
checked against it on every case in the suite, and it has disagreed, which is
the point.

\subsection{Grade 2}

Grade 2 is contracted braille, and it is what Sindhi braille books actually use.
The implementation covers 237 contractions in six prefix series plus a set of
abbreviations, and six \sd{ڳانڊڙا} groups written inside a word. The six prefix
series are Louis Braille's seventh line, $\{4,5,6,45,46,56,456\}$, of which six
of seven head a series here.

The material states the contractions but nowhere states \emph{when} a
contraction may be used. Placement rules are therefore not implemented, and we
record that as an omission in the source rather than in our reading of it.

\section{Verification}

\subsection{The design}

Five levels, each catching what the others cannot.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{The software checks itself.} Round-trip fidelity, internal
      consistency, rebuild determinism.
\item \textbf{The software against the printed standard.} Every worked example
      the guide prints, reproduced cell for cell.
\item \textbf{The software against codes written by other people.} Arabic,
      Persian and Urdu \texttt{liblouis} tables, none of which have any
      authority over Sindhi but all of which share most of its letters.
\item \textbf{A sighted check by the author of the code.} The second author
      reading dot numbers.
\item \textbf{A reading by touch, from embossed paper, cold.}
\end{enumerate}

Levels 1 to 3 can be run by anyone in minutes. Level 5 is the only one that
settles anything, and it consumes a person's time and goodwill, which is why the
earlier levels exist.

\subsection{What the suite reports}
\label{sec:suite}

\VerificationTable

\NChecksPassed{} of \NChecks{} pass on a machine without \texttt{liblouis}
installed; with it, all \NChecks{} pass. Two figures deserve comment.

\paragraph{Round-trip fidelity.} For a corpus of word types $w$ with frequencies
$f(w)$,
\[
\rho = \frac{\sum_{w} f(w)\,[\,T^{-1}(T(w)) = w\,]}{\sum_{w} f(w)}.
\]
Measured over 23{,}432 tokens (2{,}702 types) drawn from the committee's own
publications, $\rho = 0.9994$. The residue is four spellings, of which the
principal one is an abbreviation whose reading provably requires sentence
context.

\paragraph{Grade 2.} 238 of 243 contractions survive both directions. The five
that do not are cells the book itself assigns to two different words. They are a
property of the code, not a defect of the implementation, and we report them as
such.

\subsection{Corroboration from unrelated codes}

Sindhi shares most of its letters with Arabic, Persian and Urdu, whose
\texttt{liblouis} tables were written by other people, for other languages,
years before this project. Where three unrelated codes independently place a
letter in the cell we place it, a transcription slip on our part is unlikely.

Of 99 shared letters, 94 agree. Every one of the five disagreements has a reason
visible in the alphabet. Arabic gives \sd{پ}, \sd{چ} and \sd{گ} the cells that
Sindhi has already spent on \sd{ب}, \sd{ج} and \sd{ڪ}; Arabic has no \sd{ڪ} and
treats the other three as borrowings, while Sindhi treats them as native.
Persian and Urdu write \sd{ک} as dots 1-3, which in Sindhi is \sd{ڪ}, a letter
neither language has; Sindhi therefore cannot reuse the cell and marks its second
$k$ by adding \sd{ھ}, giving two cells.

That last disagreement is worth dwelling on, because \sd{ک} is the one letter
this project got wrong. The printed guide's dots appeared on four pages to show a
single cell. The second author's own chart and his printed Grade 2 book both give
two. We followed the books, and Persian and Urdu braille, which neither of us
wrote, corroborate them. The second author confirmed it directly on 15 August
2026. The printed guide's dots on those pages are a typesetting fault, not a
rule.

\subsection{The reading}

On 15 August 2026 the second author was given an embossed page produced by this
software: a passage of Sindhi news prose he had not seen, six sentences, carrying
proper nouns, digits, foreign names and a comma-heavy structure. He read it
through by touch. No corrections, no hesitation, nothing skipped.

This is the only check in the project that comes from outside it. Everything else
is one implementation checking another, or a machine checking a book.

It establishes that the code as this software writes it is readable as Sindhi
across ordinary running prose. It does not establish that every rule is right. It
was one reader and one page, and the passage carried no verse, no arithmetic and
no contractions.

\subsubsection{What the reading found}

Six observations came out of it. Two were settled on the spot, two are
implemented, two remain open.

The most useful was not about the code at all. Words were being split across
lines on the embossed page. The cause was that the file was written at 40 cells
per line, the international braille-paper width, and the page was A4, which fits
28. The embosser received lines longer than the paper and broke them itself, and
a machine breaking a line does not know where a word ends. \textbf{A braille file
has to be written at the width of the machine that will emboss it; there is no
such thing as a width-neutral braille file.} We record this because it is exactly
the class of error that no amount of self-consistency checking can catch, and it
was found in ten seconds by a person with the paper in his hands.

He also ruled on a question software cannot answer. Sindhi \sd{ک} and Urdu
\sd{ک} are one Unicode character, worth two cells in Sindhi and one in Urdu.
Asked whether a borrowed Urdu word should be written the Urdu way, he ruled that
it should not: a Sindhi reader reads that letter the same way whichever language
the word came from. One script, one value per letter, and the software never
branches on the language of a word. The alternative would have required inferring
a word's language in order to choose a cell, which software cannot do reliably.

\section{Where the printed standard contradicts itself}
\label{sec:contradictions}

Four points. None is ours to resolve; all are matters for the Sindhi Language
Authority. We report them because an implementation forces them into the open and
silence would make our choice look like the standard's.

\paragraph{Fractions.} Pages 52 and 53 state the rule twice and work nine
examples: numerator in upper digits, denominator in lower digits, no bar, and the
numerator dropped when it is 1. Page 50 instead writes fractions with a slash
cell between two upper digits, and states no rule. We implement the pp.\ 52--53
rule.

\paragraph{Brackets.} Page 32 gives one set of bracket cells for prose. Page 53
gives an entirely different set for arithmetic, and prints the open square
bracket with the same cell as the open round bracket, which must be a slip. Prose
and arithmetic may legitimately differ; the slip is separate.

\paragraph{One cell, two signs.} Page 31 prints dot 6 for both \sd{شد} and
\sd{بہ زبرون}.

\paragraph{Multiplication and the foreign-word mark.} Both are dots 5-6 followed
by dots 2-3-6, on pages 49 and 46 respectively. Our translator separates them by
spacing, since the foreign mark is attached to its word and a bare two-cell
sequence between two numbers is therefore multiplication. That rule works on
everything we have, but it is ours and not the standard's.

\section{Limitations}

\paragraph{One reader.} Every confirmation in this project traces to one person,
who is also an author of the code and of this paper. That is a strength for
authority and a weakness for independence. A second Sindhi braille reader, at a
different school, reading our sheets cold, is the most valuable missing evidence.

\paragraph{No external corpus of braille.} Both of our implementations were
written by the same person from the same documents, so their agreement proves
consistency and not correctness. A body of Sindhi braille produced by somebody
else, as a file, would break that circle. We have not obtained one.

\paragraph{Parts of the guide unseen.} We have not seen the guide's own alphabet
table or its final pages, and cannot say what is on them.

\paragraph{Grade 2 placement.} Implemented as a set of contractions, not as a
policy for when to contract, because the source states the former and not the
latter.

\paragraph{Points still being settled.} Four questions are with the second
author on an embossed decision sheet: the spacing of arithmetic, the position of
the shadda in \sd{الله}, the treatment of a line-end in verse, and the reading of
\sd{۽}. Nothing has been changed in the software in anticipation of his answers.
